sections.title: 1. The Business Cycle (LO 9.a)
sections.overview: The business cycle describes recurring fluctuations in aggregate economic activity, measured primarily by real GDP. The SIE tests the four phases in order and the technical definition of recession. Cycles vary in length and amplitude but follow a predictable sequence.
key_concepts: Four phases (in order): Expansion → Peak → Contraction → Trough → (new expansion).
Expansion: rising GDP, falling unemployment, rising consumer spending, increasing corporate profits, rising inflation pressure.
Peak: the top of the cycle; growth slows, capacity constraints, inflation typically highest.
Contraction: declining GDP, rising unemployment, falling corporate earnings, weakening demand.
Trough: bottom of the cycle; activity stabilizes before recovery.
Recession: commonly defined as two consecutive quarters of negative real GDP growth.
Depression: a prolonged, severe recession (commonly cited as six or more consecutive quarters of GDP decline).
Recovery: early expansion following a trough.
formulas: Real GDP growth = (GDP this period − GDP prior period) / GDP prior period
Recession (rule of thumb) = 2 consecutive quarters of negative real GDP growth
mnemonics: Phases in order: "Every Peak Comes Tumbling" = Expansion, Peak, Contraction, Trough.

sections.title: 2. Economic Indicators (LO 9.b)
sections.overview: Indicators are classified by their timing relative to the business cycle. The SIE expects mastery of which series lead, lag, or move with the economy, plus the principal inflation gauges.
key_concepts: Leading indicators (turn BEFORE the economy): S&P 500 stock prices, building permits/housing starts, new manufacturing orders, average weekly manufacturing hours, initial jobless claims (inverted), money supply (M2), yield curve spread, consumer expectations.
Coincident indicators (turn WITH the economy): non-farm payroll employment, personal income less transfer payments, industrial production, manufacturing & trade sales.

Lagging indicators (turn AFTER the economy): average duration of unemployment, CPI for services, change in labor cost per unit of output, ratio of consumer credit to personal income, commercial & industrial loans outstanding, average prime rate.
Inflation indicators: Consumer Price Index (CPI) — basket of consumer goods/services; Producer Price Index (PPI) — wholesale prices; GDP deflator.
Inflation: general rise in prices; erodes purchasing power and bond values.
Deflation: general decline in prices; associated with contractions.
Stagflation: stagnant growth combined with high inflation.
formulas: Inflation rate = (CPI this period − CPI prior period) / CPI prior period
Real return = Nominal return − Inflation rate
mnemonics: Leading = "Stocks, Starts, Orders, Hours, Claims, Money" — markets and manufacturing move first.
Lagging = "PUCCP": Prime rate, Unemployment duration, Consumer credit ratio, CPI services, Commercial loans.

sections.title: 3. Industry Classifications: Cyclical, Defensive, Countercyclical, Growth (LO 9.c)
sections.overview: Equity sectors respond differently to the business cycle. Knowing which industries are sensitive to expansion vs. contraction is foundational for suitability and portfolio construction questions.
key_concepts: Cyclical industries: revenues track the business cycle — outperform in expansion, suffer in contraction. Examples: autos, steel, construction, heavy machinery, airlines, luxury goods, durable goods.
Defensive (non-cyclical) industries: relatively stable demand regardless of cycle. Examples: utilities, food/consumer staples, pharmaceuticals, tobacco, basic apparel.
Countercyclical industries: move opposite to the cycle — improve when the economy weakens. Examples: discount retailers, certain debt collectors, gold mining (historically).
Growth industries: revenues grow faster than the overall economy regardless of cycle (e.g., technology, biotech); reinvest earnings, often pay little/no dividend.
Effect on equity markets: cyclicals lead in early recovery; defensives outperform late cycle and in recession.
Effect on bond markets: falling rates (typical of contraction/easy Fed policy) push bond prices up; rising rates (expansion/tightening) push prices down.
mnemonics: "Cyclical = Cars" (autos, durable goods); "Defensive = Dinner" (food, drugs, utilities — what you buy in any economy).

sections.title: 4. Financial Statements: Balance Sheet & Income Statement (LO 9.d)
sections.overview: Issuer fundamentals are disclosed primarily through the balance sheet (a snapshot) and income statement (a period of results). The SIE expects identification of each statement's components and the fundamental accounting equation.
key_concepts: Balance Sheet: snapshot of financial position at a point in time. Shows Assets, Liabilities, and Stockholders' Equity.
Assets: current (cash, receivables, inventory) and long-term/fixed (PP&E, intangibles).
Liabilities: current (payables, short-term debt, accrued expenses) and long-term (bonds, long-term loans).
Stockholders' Equity: par value of stock, additional paid-in capital, retained earnings, treasury stock (contra).
Income Statement (P&L): performance over a period — revenues minus expenses producing net income.
Key lines: Revenue → Cost of Goods Sold → Gross Profit → Operating Expenses → Operating Income → Interest & Taxes → Net Income → EPS.
Working capital: liquidity measure; positive value indicates ability to meet short-term obligations.
Retained earnings link the two statements: prior RE + Net Income − Dividends = ending RE.
rules: Securities Exchange Act of 1934 §12 requires issuers listing on a national securities exchange to file balance sheets and profit-and-loss statements (up to 3 preceding fiscal years), certified as required by SEC rules.
formulas: Accounting Equation: Assets = Liabilities + Stockholders' Equity
Working Capital = Current Assets − Current Liabilities
Current Ratio = Current Assets / Current Liabilities
Quick (Acid-Test) Ratio = (Current Assets − Inventory) / Current Liabilities
Operating Income = Gross Profit − Operating Expenses
Net Income = Operating Income − Interest − Taxes
EPS = (Net Income − Preferred Dividends) / Common Shares Outstanding
Retained Earnings (ending) = Retained Earnings (beginning) + Net Income − Dividends
mnemonics: Income Statement = "REV-EX = NET" — Revenues minus Expenses equals Net income.

sections.title: 5. Principal Economic Theories: Keynesian vs. Monetarist/Supply-Side (LO 9.e)
sections.overview: Two macroeconomic schools drive policy debates and exam questions. Keynesians emphasize aggregate demand and fiscal intervention; monetarists/supply-siders emphasize money supply and incentives.
key_concepts: Keynesian Economics (John Maynard Keynes): aggregate demand drives output and employment; government should use fiscal policy (spending and taxation) to smooth the business cycle. Advocates deficit spending in recession.

Monetarist Economics (Milton Friedman): money supply growth is the dominant driver of output in the short run and inflation in the long run. Favors stable, rule-based monetary policy by the central bank.
Supply-Side Economics: lower taxes and reduced regulation increase production incentives, expanding aggregate supply and stimulating growth; associated with the Laffer curve.
Fiscal Policy: tools of Congress and the President — taxation and government spending.
Monetary Policy: tools of the Federal Reserve — controls money supply and short-term interest rates.

sections.title: 6. International Economics: Exchange Rates and Balance of Trade (LO 9.f)
sections.overview: Currency values and trade flows affect U.S. issuers, investors in foreign securities, and bond markets. The SIE expects understanding of how exchange-rate changes impact exports, imports, and the balance of payments.
key_concepts: Exchange Rate: price of one currency in terms of another; determined largely by supply and demand in FX markets.
Strong U.S. dollar: imports cheaper for U.S. consumers; U.S. exports more expensive abroad; hurts U.S. exporters, helps importers and foreign-goods consumers.
Weak U.S. dollar: U.S. exports cheaper abroad (boosts exporters); imports more expensive; can stoke inflation.
Balance of Trade: exports minus imports of goods/services. Surplus = exports > imports; deficit = imports > exports. The U.S. typically runs a trade deficit.
Balance of Payments: broader measure — current account (trade + income + transfers) + capital/financial account. Must balance overall.
GDP: total value of goods/services produced WITHIN a country's borders.
GNP: total value of goods/services produced by a country's residents/nationals regardless of location.
Foreign investment impact: rising U.S. interest rates attract foreign capital, strengthening the dollar; falling rates weaken it.
formulas: GDP = C + I + G + (X − M)   where C=consumption, I=investment, G=gov't spending, X=exports, M=imports
mnemonics: Strong dollar: "IN-cheap, EX-pensive" — Imports cheap, Exports pricey.
Weak dollar: "EX-cellent, IM-possible" — Exports thrive, Imports cost more.

sections.title: 7. Purpose and Structure of the Federal Reserve (LO 9.g)
sections.overview: The Federal Reserve is the central bank of the United States, charged by Congress with a dual mandate: maximum employment and stable prices. It regulates banks, supervises the payment system, and conducts monetary policy.
key_concepts: Dual mandate: (1) maximum sustainable employment, (2) price stability (targeting ~2% inflation).
Structure: Board of Governors (7 members appointed by the President, confirmed by Senate, 14-year terms); 12 regional Federal Reserve Banks.

FOMC (Federal Open Market Committee): sets monetary policy — composed of the 7 Governors + President of the NY Fed (permanent voter) + 4 rotating regional Reserve Bank presidents (12 voting members total).
Fed is independent of the executive branch but reports to Congress.
Fed regulates member banks, sets reserve and capital requirements, acts as lender of last resort, and operates the payment system.

sections.title: 8. Active Tools of Federal Reserve Monetary Policy (LO 9.h)
sections.overview: The Fed influences money supply, credit conditions, and short-term rates through several tools. Open market operations are by far the most active tool used day-to-day; interest on reserve balances (IORB) now serves as the principal policy rate floor.
key_concepts: Open Market Operations (OMO): FOMC-directed buying/selling of U.S. Treasury securities in the secondary market. MOST ACTIVE tool.
Fed BUYS securities → adds reserves to banking system → money supply ↑ → interest rates ↓ → EASING policy.
Fed SELLS securities → drains reserves → money supply ↓ → interest rates ↑ → TIGHTENING policy.
Discount Rate: rate charged to member banks on short-term loans from the Fed's discount window. Raised to tighten, cut to ease. A directly set (not market-determined) rate.

Reserve Requirements: historically required percentage of deposits banks must hold in reserve. Reserve-requirement ratio was set to 0% effective March 26, 2020 and remains 0% — therefore reserve requirements are NOT currently an active policy tool.
Interest on Reserve Balances (IORB): rate the Fed pays banks on reserves held at the Fed; now the principal administered policy rate that anchors the federal funds rate range.
Federal Funds Target Range: set by the FOMC; market federal funds rate is influenced by IORB (floor) and discount-window pricing.
Moral suasion: informal Fed pressure/jawboning to influence bank behavior.
mnemonics: BUY = Bigger money supply, Yields down (easing). SELL = Slimmer money supply, yields up (tightening).
Fed tools today: "OMO + Discount + IORB" (reserve requirements at 0% — dormant).

sections.title: 9. Four Prominent Interest Rates (LO 9.i)
sections.overview: Four short-term rates dominate exam questions, ranked from lowest to highest under normal conditions. Knowing which is set by the Fed vs. determined by markets, and who borrows/lends, is critical.
key_concepts: Federal Funds Rate: rate banks charge EACH OTHER for overnight loans of reserves. Market-determined within the FOMC's target range. Most volatile.
Discount Rate: rate the FED charges member BANKS borrowing at the discount window. Set directly by the Federal Reserve Board.
Broker Call (Call Money) Rate: rate banks charge BROKER-DEALERS for loans collateralized by securities; basis for margin loan rates passed to customers.
Prime Rate: rate large commercial banks charge their MOST CREDITWORTHY corporate customers. Set by banks; tends to move with the federal funds rate.
Typical ranking (lowest → highest): Federal Funds < Discount < Broker Call < Prime. (Exam often emphasizes Fed Funds as the lowest among these.)
LIBOR: historically a global benchmark; being phased out in favor of SOFR (Secured Overnight Financing Rate) — not a Fed-set rate.
formulas: Customer margin rate ≈ Broker Call Rate + broker's spread
mnemonics: "Fred Drove By Paul" — Fed funds, Discount, Broker call, Prime (low → high).
Who pays whom: Fed Funds = bank↔bank; Discount = Fed→bank; Broker Call = bank→broker; Prime = bank→best customer.

sections.title: 10. Monetary vs. Fiscal Policy — Synthesis
sections.overview: The SIE distinguishes who controls each lever and what each can accomplish. Monetary policy is the Fed's domain; fiscal policy belongs to Congress and the President.
key_concepts: Monetary Policy: controlled by the FEDERAL RESERVE. Tools: OMO, discount rate, IORB, (reserve requirements — currently 0%). Targets money supply and short-term rates.
Fiscal Policy: controlled by CONGRESS and the PRESIDENT. Tools: government spending and taxation. Affects aggregate demand directly.
Expansionary monetary policy: Fed buys securities, lowers discount rate → ↑ money supply, ↓ rates → stimulates economy → bond prices ↑, equities typically benefit.
Contractionary monetary policy: Fed sells securities, raises discount rate → ↓ money supply, ↑ rates → cools economy → bond prices ↓.
Expansionary fiscal policy: increased spending or tax cuts → stimulates demand; may increase deficits.
Contractionary fiscal policy: reduced spending or higher taxes → slows demand; reduces deficits.
Yield Curve: plot of yields by maturity. Normal (upward) = healthy growth; Inverted (downward) = recession signal; Flat = transitional.
mnemonics: "Fed = Money; Feds (Congress) = Money OUT/IN via tax & spend."
